feedback: D1: Your catalogue is clean and evidence-led, and you correctly held the line that a finding only counts when a request, response, or token proves it. You nailed SQL injection (A03/CWE-89 with the admin' OR '1'='1 to 302 line), JWT alg:none (Token 2, accept that CWE-345 stands in for CWE-347), missing token lifecycle (CWE-613, exp:9999999999), stored XSS to the 185.220.101.9:8443 cookie beacon, path traversal returning root:x:0:0, and open redirect. That is six of the ten. You lost real ground by omitting the unsalted MD5 hashing (A02/CWE-916), the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (A05/CWE-798), the XXE in 04-import-xxe.xml (you caught it in D3 but not the D1 table), and the cookie missing Secure/SameSite (CWE-614). Your decoy verdict picked a defensible target in the HS256 Token 3 signature and said it was not exploitable, which is the right direction, but you proved it only by absence of a bypass in the logs rather than at the mechanism level. The full-credit answer is that the HS256 verify branch uses hash_equals(), which is constant-time, so that branch is genuinely sound, and the real bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret. D2: The chain runs in the correct order from SQLi through user enumeration, XSS, open redirect, and file read, and your PoC payloads are verbatim and traceable, which is the strongest part of this deliverable. Two gaps cost you. Your CVSS vectors are bare, with scores but no justifying sentence per finding, and that caps the vector row at half on its own, and your SQLi vector reads A:H for a 9.8 when the bypass does not touch availability, so the defensible value is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. Your business impact in D2 stops at 312 records with no naira, no balances up to ~950k NGN summing to tens of millions, and no stated assumptions, and you did not surface the senior insight that a forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service for an S:C scope change. The XXE hop and the explicit 312-row exfil hop are also missing from the chain itself. D3: This is your best work. The executive summary is jargon-free and lands on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model correctly names the external actor and the internal /api/v1/internal trust, findings are tied to capture timestamps, and your remediation table is genuinely ordered by effort to risk rather than by CVSS, with the earliest-break fix called out at the login query. Your two detection stopgaps are concrete with exact fields and false-positive rates. Two things hurt: several OWASP labels drift in D3 (XXE shown as A03 not A05, open redirect as A10 not A01, XSS as A07 not A03, though your CWEs are right), and your decoy paragraph reframes the secret and MD5 as low-hanging fruit that was not the attack path, which is not the disproved-decoy the brief asks for; the safe construct to state is the hash_equals HS256 branch. D4: You answer all four prompts in your own voice, cite ISC2 Canon I by number in a load-bearing way, and anchor to your own reconstruction of the chain, which is exactly the move. You name the NDPA duty to notify the authority and the affected individuals but do not give the section numbers; cite NDPA 2023 section 40 (notify NDPC within 72 hours) and section 41 (notify data subjects on high risk) tied to the 312 customers. One flag for your records: the D4 header reads 'abel rose, UBI-2026-002' while D1 to D3 are under your name and UBI-2026-0041, so check you submitted the right file. I looked for room to round up and the readable evidence supports 71 honestly, no higher, because four D1 findings are simply absent and the D2 CVSS vectors carry no justification. The single most important fix: justify every CVSS vector with one sentence and correct the SQLi vector to A:N (about 9.1), and quantify impact in naira with stated assumptions, not a bare record count.
